Resettlement · Uganda

Dated structure records for RAP cut-off dates in Uganda

Uganda’s Constitution requires compensation to be paid before land is taken, so the dates in a resettlement process carry weight for everyone involved. We map the structures in your project footprint on dated imagery, before the census, at the cut-off date and after it, so the RAP team, the valuer and the lender work from the same record. A person reviews every result.

Used in: Oil & gas · Power & utilities · Rail & roads · Project finance & ESIA

Request a proposal See the sample register

What the law asks for

Compensation before possession, and the occupants the law protects

A summary of the public rules as of 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

The Constitution and the Supreme Court

Compulsory acquisition needs a public use and “prompt payment of fair and adequate compensation, prior to the taking of possession” (Constitution, art. 26(2)(b)(i)). In UNRA v Irumba & Another [2015] UGSC 131, the Supreme Court agreed that “Section 7 of the Land Acquisition Act is inconsistent with Article 26(2)”; the Constitutional Court had nullified s.7(1) ([2013] UGCC 17) to the extent that it allowed possession before payment.

The Land Acquisition Act

Compulsory acquisitions are declared by statutory instrument under the Land Acquisition Act 1965 (Cap. 235). UETCL’s resettlement framework notes that the Act “does not define specific timelines for payment of compensation, nor does it provide for adjustments to compensation amounts in cases where payment is delayed”. No amendment bill is on Parliament’s tracker as of 27 September 2026.

Land tenure and occupants

“Land in Uganda belongs to the citizens of Uganda”, held under customary, freehold, mailo or leasehold tenure (art. 237). The Land Act (Cap. 236) protects lawful and bona fide occupants, including bibanja holders on mailo land, and UETCL’s resettlement framework treats them as eligible for compensation.

Compensation and valuation

As UETCL’s framework summarises the Land Act as enacted, compensation is at depreciated replacement cost in rural areas or market value in urban areas, plus a disturbance allowance of 15 %, or 30 % where less than six months’ notice to give vacant possession is given. District compensation rates for crops and trees follow current local market value (Land Regulations 2004, reg 24(1)). The Valuation Bill 2024 was assented to on 19 February 2026; it creates the office of the Chief Government Valuer and a professional institute for valuers.

Lender standards

Projects financed by the World Bank apply ESS5, which UETCL’s framework describes as compensation “prior to displacement, at full replacement cost”, with amounts “adjusted to reflect current values” where payment is delayed. Other lenders apply IFC Performance Standard 5, which ties eligibility to a census and to a cut-off date that is clearly established and made public. Under both, the dates matter, and a dated structure register supports the record of them.

How it works

Before the census, at the cut-off date, and after

Sizing

Before the census

How many structures stand in the footprint and the buffers around it, where they cluster, and estimated households with the assumptions stated, so the census and asset-inventory teams are sized and routed before they go.

The record

At the cut-off date

A register of the structures on dated imagery, with IDs, coordinates and reviewer categories such as main building, outbuilding, enclosure or under construction, packaged with file fingerprints and an independent timestamp. Categories describe what the imagery shows; they do not establish use, ownership or value, and compensation needs ground verification.

Change

After the cut-off date

Re-surveys of the footprint and of resettlement sites, with new structures since the cut-off date flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, and location checks for single grievances.

For a pipeline, a transmission line or a road, the same register first compares the route options, so the land affected by each can be weighed before a route is fixed. See pipelines, power-line wayleaves and road and railway reserves in Uganda.

Where dated imagery helps

Three moments where a date settles a question

The cut-off date

Which structures stood in the footprint on the date that fixes eligibility, and which appeared after it. The dates protect everyone’s entitlements: the occupants’ as well as the project’s.

Valuation and payment

Compensation is due before possession, and where payment is delayed the World Bank standard asks for amounts to be adjusted to current values. A re-survey before payment shows what has changed in the footprint since the valuation.

Grievances and claims

For one plot or claim, a sheet of every dated image covering it, so the grievance team sees what stood there on each date, and an evidence pack when the question goes further.

The imagery

Why the date on the imagery matters

A cut-off-date record is only as good as the date on its imagery. We build it on imagery with a known capture date: a very-high-resolution satellite scene with its acquisition date, georeferenced imagery you already hold, or a drone survey flown with the approvals each job requires. Map-service basemaps, which carry no capture date, are never used for it.

Archive coverage and cloud vary by place and season, so the proposal says what exists for your footprint and dates before you commit. A new satellite capture can be requested when the archive is too old; its date depends on satellite availability and weather, and is never guaranteed.

In Uganda a drone baseline also needs UCAA approval, Chief of Defence Forces security clearance and a district sign-off for each operation, and regulation 79 of the drone regulations requires the owner’s consent before private property is imaged in a way that could amount to keeping it under observation. See drone law in Uganda.

What you receive

  • A structure register: ID, coordinates, category and imagery date
  • Maps of the footprint and its buffers
  • A PDF report in English
  • GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers
  • An evidence pack with file fingerprints and an independent timestamp
  • Change layers and a notice after each re-survey
  • Estimated households, with the assumptions stated

Personal data

Structures on our side, names on yours

The Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 governs personal data, and census records are full of it. We keep them apart: our registers list structures with IDs and coordinates, and names, ID numbers and household data stay with your census team. Where you link the two, you do it on your side, through the structure IDs.

People and vehicles in any drone imagery are blurred, deliverables go only to the recipients you name in writing, and nothing about the project area is published. Processing or storing personal data outside Uganda needs adequate protection in the destination or the data subject’s consent, which is one more reason to keep personal data out of the imagery work.

Who uses it

RAP teams, their consultants, and the people who check their work

Land acquisition and RAP teams

On pipeline, power, road, railway and industrial-park projects, planning the census and keeping the cut-off-date record.

ESIA, RAP and valuation firms

Sizing the census, comparing route options and checking the field inventory, in the formats their teams already use.

Lenders and independent monitors

Checking between site visits what has changed in the footprint and at resettlement sites since the cut-off date.

Limits

What a cut-off baseline is not

What it supports

  • Census and asset-inventory planning
  • Cut-off-date records under the Land Acquisition Act, ESS5 and IFC Performance Standard 5
  • Valuation checks and grievance handling, with dated facts
  • Comparison of route and site options

What it does not do

  • Set the cut-off date or decide who is eligible
  • Carry out the census, the valuation or the consultations
  • Record tenure: kibanja, mailo, customary or leasehold rights come from the land records and the census
  • Count crops or trees, identify households or people, or see roofs hidden under dense tree cover

Frequently asked questions

Does the imagery set the cut-off date?

No. The cut-off date comes from the project’s resettlement process and the lender’s standard, and it must be clearly established and made public. Our register records what stood in the footprint on the imagery date closest to it; it supports the cut-off-date record rather than defining it.

Are bibanja holders and other occupants in the register?

The register lists structures, not people or tenure. Who holds a kibanja, who is a lawful or bona fide occupant and who is eligible for what are for the census, the land records and the valuer. The register tells those teams where each structure is, and whether it stood on the cut-off date.

Is the register a substitute for the census or the asset inventory?

No. The census, the inventory of structures, crops and trees, the valuation and the consultations stay with your RAP team and the valuer. The register sizes and routes that work, and shows which structures appeared after the cut-off date.

Can you check a single grievance?

Yes. For one point or claim we prepare a sheet of every dated image covering it, so your grievance team can see what stood there on each date. What the grievance committee decides is for it and the parties.

Can the baseline come from drone imagery?

Where a drone survey is flown with the approvals and security clearances each job requires, yes. In Uganda that means UCAA approval, Chief of Defence Forces clearance and a district sign-off for each operation, so most baselines start from dated satellite scenes or imagery you already hold.

Do you hold names or ID numbers of project-affected persons?

No. Names, ID numbers and household data stay with your census team. We map structures, and the register links to your census only through the structure IDs you choose to use.

Setting a cut-off date in Uganda?

Tell us the footprint, the census window and the date the record must reflect. We reply with the dated imagery that exists for it and a written proposal.
